Sorry it had to be like this. // Nothing personal. // No hard feelings.
badly + don't think.
column5: The nuance is almost "sorry," or "forgive me." The speaker probably is about to (or just did) do something bad [e.g. kill] his opponent, and he's saying, "Don't think poorly of me for this, because I didn't really have much of a choice." Or at least, that

column3:
Sorry.
forgive [me], ね
column5: You could say this to a friend, for example, if you were late to meet with them, in which case it would get translated to "Sorry I'm late." The nuance, however, is that you're not all that sorry.

column2: 許してくれ！
column3:
Forgive me!
forgive [me] + くれ！
column5: For example, if you accidentally killed your friend due to some dispute or problem, afterwards you could hold their lifeless body and yell this to them.

column2: ごめんね。
column3:
Sorry.
sorry + ね.
column5: A nice, friendly, causal way to say "sorry." You sound more sorry than if you had said 許してね [yurushite ne], but less sorry than if you'd said the polite ごめんなさい [gomennasai].

column2: ついてないな。
column3:
I have bad luck. // What bad luck.
not sticking [?] + な
column5: Adding な is common, because な is like the "inward ね," you're making this comment more to yourself than to anyone else.

column2: 最悪！
column3:
Just my luck. // Oh, great. // You're kidding me! // This is the worst.
the worst / the lowest.
column5: That "Oh, great" and "You're kidding me" are both angry and sarcastic. The rhetorical questions of one wallowing in self-pity.

column2: あー最悪！
column3:
Ah, just great!
ah + the worst.

column2: もう最悪！
column3:
I've had it!
already + the worst.
column5: It sounds like multiple bad things have been happening, but this last bad thing pushed you over the top. Again, it sounds a bit feminine.

column2: お前に俺は倒せない。
column3:
You could never defeat me. // I'm out of your league.

column2: お前には俺は倒せない。
column3:
You could never defeat me. // I'm out of your league.
You + には + I + は + can't defeat/knock down.

You could never defeat me. // I'm out of your league.
You + には + I + を + can't defeat/knock down.

column3:
You could never defeat me. // I'm out of your league.
You + は + I + を + can't defeat/knock down.
column5: The nuance, perhaps obviously, is that 'you' are too weak to defeat 'me.'

column2: 何か俺に出来ることがあったらなんでも言ってね。
column3:
If there's anything at all that I can do, please let me know.
something + I + に + can do + thing + が + is if + anything + say + ね
column5: For example, when trying to comfort someone that has had something really bad happen to them.

column2: 明日からバケーションなんだ。

I'm going on vacation tomorrow!
tomorrow + from + vacation + なん + is.

column2: いいなー。
column3:
That sounds amazing. // I'm jealous.
good + なー.

column2: 羨ましいなー。
column3:
I'm jealous. // Ah, I'm so jealous.
jealous + なー.

column2: 羨ましいね。
column3:
He's so lucky, huh?
jealous + ね.
column5: To make this translation work, we have to add a third person. So we have (A) the person going on vacation, (B) the person talking, and (C) the person being spoken to. The nuance is "You and I are jealous of him, huh?

column2: 《看板》 入場女性無料！男性1000円
column3:
《sign》 Girls get in free! Guys 1,000 yen.
sign + entry/admission + females + free! + males + 1000 + yen.
column5: This is, for example, a sign that you might see outside of a small club in Tokyo somewhere.

column2: 不公平だ！
column3:
No fair!
unfair + is!

column2: 明日イケメンと合コンなんだ。
column3:
I'm going on a group date with some good-looking guys tomorrow.
tomorrow + good-looking guy + with + goukon + なん + is.
column5: A 合コン is kind of like a group blind date. Usually it starts with 1 guy and 1 girl that know each other, then they set up a dinner date with an additional 2 guys and 2 girls, and the six of them chat and hang out. In the U.S., I think you'd just invite eac

column2: ずるい！
column3:
No fair!
sly / dishonest / sneaky / crafty!
column5: I think this sounds just a bit feminine.

column2: 愛妻弁当か？ずるいなー。
column3:
Your wife made you lunch? Lucky...
beloved wife bento + か? + sly + なー.
column5: 愛妻弁当 is pretty much one word--it refers to a bento box prepared [with loving care] by one's wife.

column2: 夜ご飯どうする？
column3:
What should we do for dinner? // What do you want to do for dinner?
dinner + how + do?

column2: このあとどうする？
column3:
What do you wanna do after this? // What should we do after this?
after this + how + do?
column5: For example, when deciding what to do with one or more friends after dinner [and you're currently at dinner when you say this].

column2: 明日どうする？
column3:
What do you wanna do tomorrow? // What should we do tomorrow?
tomorrow + how + do?

column2: 週末どうする？
column3:
What do you wanna do this weekend? // What should we do this weekend?
weekend + how + do?

column2: 飲み会どうする？
column3:
When should we have the (drinking) party? // Do you wanna go to that (drinking) party, then? // Who should we invite to the (drinking) party? // What type of place should we choose for the (drinking) party? // Where should we have the (drinking) party? //
[drinking] party + how + do?
column5: Sorry for getting a little crazy with translations there. The reason is that the meaning of this sentence will depend on the context. This just goes to show how versatile [and simplistic] casual Japanese can be.

column2: 週末何する？
column3: What do you wanna do this weekend? // What should we do this weekend?

column2: 今日はどうなさいますか。
column3:
So how would you like it?
today + は + how + do + か.
column5: A hairdresser could say this to a client before cutting their hair, for example.

column2: 焼肉にしよう。
column3:
Let's get yakiniku.
yakiniku + に + let's do.

column2: 帰ろう。
column3:
Let's go home. // Let's call it a night.
let's go home.
column5: A and B may or may not live together.

column2: やっぱりやめよう。
column3:
Yeah, let's not go, after all. // Yeah, let's not do (that thing), after all.
on second thought + let's quit.
column5: The nuance is that A and B were previously planning to do something tomorrow, but B doesn't think they should anymore.

column2: 飲みに行こう。
column3:
Let's go out.
drink + に + let's go.
column5: Actually, this means "Let's go drinking," but I think that sounds a bit more intense in English.

column2: 金曜日にしよう。
column3:
Let's have it on Friday.
Friday + に + let's do.

column2: あの安いとこ行こうよ。
column3:
Let's go to that cheap place.
that + cheap + place + let's go + よ.
column5: Adding よ onto the end just sounds like you really want to go there.

column2: どうしようか。
column3:
Hmm... What should we do...
how + let's do + か.

column2: ミホは？
column3: What do you think, Miho?

column2: ミホはどこがいい？
column3:
Where do you think we should go, Miho?
Miho + は + where + が + good?

column2: ミホは何がいい？
column3:
What do you feel like, Miho?
Miho + は + what + が + good?

column2: フランス行きたい。
column3:
I want to go to France.
France + want to go.

column2: 居酒屋行きたい。
column3:
I want to go to an izakaya.
izakaya + want to go.

column2: ラーメン食べたい！
column3:
I want to eat ramen!
ramen + want to eat.

column2: 日本語話したい。
column3:
I want to speak Japanese.
Japanese + want to speak.
column5: This sounds like (1) you are able to speak Japanese, and (2) you want to use Japanese [not learn it].

column2: 日本語話せるようになりたい。
column3:
I want to learn to speak Japanese.
Japanese + can speak + ように + want to become.
column5: That's "potential VERB + ように + VERB～たい.

column2: フランス行きたいな～。
column3:
I want to go to France.
France + want to go + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I probably can't go to France [anytime soon].

column2: 居酒屋行きたいな～。
column3:
I want to go to an izakaya.
izakaya + want to go + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I probably can't go to an izakaya [anytime soon].

column2: ラーメン食べたいな～！
column3:
I want to eat ramen!
ramen + want to eat + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I probably can't eat ramen [anytime soon].

column2: 日本語話したいな～。
column3:
I want to speak Japanese.
Japanese + want to speak + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I probably don't have anyone to speak Japanese with at the moment.

column2: 日本語話せるようになりたいな～。
column3:
I want to learn to speak Japanese.
Japanese + can speak + ように + want to become + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I am still a long way from being able to speak Japanese.

column2: フランス行ってみたい。
column3:
I'd like to go to France.
France + go [and] + want to see.
column5: The nuance is something like, "I want to go to France... if I ever get the chance," but I'm not necessarily going out of my way to make the chance.

column2: 居酒屋行ってみたい。
column3:
I'd like to go to an izakaya (for the first time).
izakaya + go [and] + want to see.
column5: The nuance is that I've never been to an izakaya... which makes it rare for a Japanese person to say.

column2: ラーメン食べてみたい！
column3:
I want to try ramen!
ramen + eat [and] + want to see.
column5: The nuance is that I've never eaten ramen before... maybe because I'm a tourist?

column2: 日本語話してみたい。
column3:
I want to try speaking Japanese.
Japanese + speak [and] + want to see.
column5: This sounds like either [A] I want to try speaking Japanese for the first time or [B] I want to try speaking Japanese [with someone], but I don't know if I'm good enough to do so.

column2: 日本語話せるようになってみたい。
column3:
I wish I could speak Japanese. // It'd be cool if I could speak Japanese.
Japanese + can speak + ように + become [and] + want to see.
column5: This sounds like I don't really believe myself capable of learning to speak Japanese... and maybe I won't even study.

column2: フランス行ってみたいな～。
column3:
I'd like to go to France.
France + go [and] + want to see + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I can't... maybe because plane tickets are expensive and I'm poor?

column2: 居酒屋行ってみたいな～。
column3:
I'd like to go to an izakaya (for the first time).
izakaya + go [and] + want to see + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I can't... maybe because I'm not in Japan?

column2: ラーメン食べてみたいな～！
column3:
I want to try ramen!
ramen + eat [and] + want to see + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I can't... maybe because I'm not in Japan?

column2: 日本語話してみたいな～。
column3:
I want to try speaking Japanese.
Japanese + speak [and] + want to see + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I've never had a chance to speak it before... and I don't know when I'll get one, either.

column2: 日本語話せるようになってみたいな～。
column3:
I wish I could speak Japanese. // It'd be cool if I could speak Japanese.
Japanese + can speak + ように + become [and] + want to see + な～.
column5: The nuance is that I have super low confidence in my ability to do so.

column3:
When do you want to eat? // When are you going to eat?
when + eat?

column3:
I think I'll take a shower. // I'm gonna take a shower.
shower + let's bathe/shower
column5: It's like you're thinking out loud: "Hey, self, let's shower.

column2: 後で食べよう。
column3:
I think I'll eat (this) later. // I'm gonna eat this later.
later + let's eat

column2: もうちょっと寝よう。
column3:
I think I'll sleep a little longer. // I'm gonna sleep a little longer.
a little more + let's sleep

column3:
I think I'll buy this. // I'm gonna buy this.
this + let's buy

column2: シャワー浴びようかな～。
column3:
Hmm... maybe I'll take a shower...
shower + let's bathe/shower + かな～

column2: 後で食べようかな～。
column3:
Hmm... maybe I'll eat (this) later.
later + let's eat + かな～

column2: もうちょっと寝ようかな～。
column3:
Hmm... maybe I'll sleep a little longer.
a little more + let's sleep + かな～

column3:
Hmm... maybe I'll buy this.
this + let's buy + かな～

column3:
So buy it, then.
if you buy it

column2: 買いなよ。
column3:
Yeah, buy it.
buy + なよ
column5: We saw this grammar form in Lesson #48 & Lesson #49! This is somewhat like saying 買えば, only, in this case, the speaker appears to also believe that buying it is a good idea.

not expensive?

column3:
Don't buy that.
quit/stop + なよ
column5: The speaker clearly thinks buying it is a bad idea.

column2: 車買おうかな～。

Hmm... maybe I'll buy a car...
car + let's buy + かな～

column3:
I think I'll buy a car...
car + let's buy.

column3:

car + let's buy + と + am thinking.
column5: Less casually, 思ってる will appear as 思っている or, even more formally, as 思っています.

column2: 今勉強してる。
column3:

now + am studying.

column3:
I've been studying recently.
recently + am studying.
column5: For both of these examples we're using してる, but less casually that's している, and formally that's しています.

column2: 会社をやめて、１年ぐらい留学しようと思っています。
column3:
I'm considering quitting my job and studying abroad for a year or so. // I've been thinking about quitting my job and studying abroad for a year or so.
company + を + quit and + one year + about + let's study abroad + と + am thinking.

column2: 会社やめて、１年ぐらい留学しようと思ってる。
column3:
I'm considering quitting my job and studying abroad for a year or so. // I've been thinking about quitting my job and studying abroad for a year or so.
company + quit and + one year + about + let's study abroad + と + am thinking.

column2: 今夜は焼肉にしようと思ってる。
column3:
I'm thinking of having [making; going to] yakiniku for dinner tonight.
tonight + は + yakiniku + に + let's do + と + am thinking.

column2: これ買おうと思う。
column3:
I think I'll buy this (jacket).
this + let's buy + と + think.

column2: これ買おーっと。
column3: I think I'll buy this.

column2: 居酒屋行こう。
column3: Let's go to an izakaya.

column2: すいません！
column3: Excuse me.
column5: You can pretty much yell this while you're in an izakaya to get a waiter's attention... for example, when you want to order. Don't expect them to come and check on you like they do in American restaurants... which is really a flawed system, if you think a

column2: 飲み放題いくらですか？
column3:
How much is the all-you-can-drink course?
all-you-can-drink + how much + is + か
column5: Replace 飲み放題 with whatever item you want to know the price of.

column2: とりあえず生二つください。
column3:
Could we get two beers to start, please?
for the time being + raw/draft + two + please.
column5: This is pretty much a set phrase at izakaya... I'm not sure why, but beer is the go-to first drink at izakaya in Japan [though I also have a lot of friends that don't drink... so don't feel pressured!].+++Those little things of food are called お通し [otoosh

column2: お通しあげる。
column3: You can have my otoshi.
column5: お通し is actually a seating fee, but it also comes with a tiny plate of food you receive when sitting down.

column2: 唐揚げ一つとフライドポテト一つください。
column3:
One order of fried chicken and one order of french fries, please.
fried chicken + one + and + french fries + one + please.
column5: Yeah, they eat a lot of fried chicken and french fries at these places. Not sure why. You can replace any food item before 一つ, or say 二つ [futatsu] if you want two, 三つ [mittsu] if you want three, and so on... save the ください for the end, because this indicat

column2: りんご三つ買ってきて。
column3: Will you go buy three apples?

column2: さつまいも食べたい。
column3: I feel like eating sweet potato. // I want to eat sweet potato.

column2: 黒蜜って何からできてんの？
column3:
What is kuromitsu made of?
kuromitsu + って + what + from + making + の？
column5: Kuromitsu is like a brown/black sugary honey. Also, this できてんの？ is a casual abbreviation of できているの？

column2: これ下げてもらえますか。
column3:
Could you take this/these away, please?
this + lower + could I receive + か.
column5: Say this when you want them to take away old plates and/or glasses.

column2: 注文いいですか。
column3:
Is it all right to order right now?
order + good + is + か.
column5: When someone comes by to drop off food at your table, for example, you can say this if you want to order something right then.

column2: お会計お願いします。
column3:
Could I get the check, please?
check + please.

column2: これ食べてみて。
column3:
Try (eating) this.

this + let's carry + か.

that + let's carry + か.

if it's good, + will carry + よ.

dark + is + ね. + electricity + will turn on + ね.

let's carry + か.

It's dark. Want me to turn on the lights?
dark + ね. + electricity + let's turn on + か.
column5: We dropped both ですね after 暗い and the を after 電気, because we cut out as many words as possible in casual Japanese! Be careful with the intonation on this one. You do NOT use rising intonation (like with a question). I suppose it's because the nuance is tha

column2: 持つよ。
column3:
I'll carry this [that].
carry + よ.

column3:
I'll carry this.
this + (will) carry + よ.

column2: それ持つよ。
column3:
I'll carry that.
that + (will) carry + よ.

column2: 暗いね。電気つけるね。
column3:
It's dark. I'll turn on the lights.
dark + ね. + electricity + (will) turn on + ね.

I'll carry that for you.
carry and + give (you) + よ.

help (out) and + give (you) + よ.

OK / all right (+ is). + thank you

teacher + に + apple + を + gave.

column2: 警察官がお母さんに傘をくれた。
column3:

police officer + が + mother + に + umbrella + を + gave.

column2: 店員さんが（私の）友達にクーポン(を)くれた。

shop member/employee + は (+ I + の) + friend + に + coupon + を + gave.

older brother + は + that + flower + を + girlfriend/she + に + gave.

column2: 先生が教えてくれた。
column3:
My teacher taught me (this).
teacher + が + teach and + gave.
column5: We're not going to talk about は and が in this article, as that's a nightmare for another day, but the reason we say が here is that we're pointing out who taught me, and が is kind of like the "pointer particle."

column2: レポート書いてあげた。
column3:
I wrote the report for him.
report + write and + gave.

column2: 「～してあげる」という言い方にムカつくのって私だけですか？
column3:
Am I the only one who gets offended when people say "~shite ageru"?
～ してあげる + という + way of saying + に + get offended / angry + の + って + I + only + is + か.

column2: 〇〇に連れていってあげる。
column3:
I'll take you to 〇〇.
〇〇 + に + take you along + give.
column5: She's using 〇〇 as a placeholder for "[place]."

column2: 今度✕✕ のお店教えてあげるね。

Next time I'll take you to XX.
this time / next time + XX + の + shop + teach and + give + ね.
column5: While earlier we saw 教える being used to mean, literally, "teach," this time it is closer to "inform" or "introduce." Or, in my translation, "take." Also, sometimes 今度 will mean "this time." Sometimes it will mean "next time." I should write a lesson on it,

column2: 一緒に○○行こう。
column3:
Let's go to 〇〇.
together + 〇〇 + let's go.

column2: 今度 ✕✕ のお店教えるね。
column3:
Next time I'll show you ✕✕.
this time / next time + ✕✕ + の + shop + teach + ね.

column2: 田中さんは起きるのが早いですね。
column3: You wake up early.

column2: 田中は毎朝ジョギングしてるって。
column3:
Tanaka said he goes jogging every morning.
Tanaka + は + every morning + jogging + is doing + って.

column2: マジ？出勤する前ってこと？
column3:
Seriously? Like, before (going to) work?
Serious? + go to work + before + って + thing?
column5: ～ってこと or ～ということ is actually grammar stuff... we'll give it a good look-over some other time.

column2: うん。起きるの早いんだって。
column3:
Yeah. He said he gets up early.
Yeah. + get up [wake up] + の + early + んだって.

column2: 俺朝苦手。
column3:
I'm not a morning person.
I + morning + poor (at).

column2: 俺も。
column3:
Me neither.
I + too.

column2: 英語喋るの難しくない？
column3:
Isn't speaking English difficult?
English + speak [chat] + の + not difficult?

column2: いや、聞き取るのが難しい。
column3:
No. What's difficult is listening. // No. Listening is the thing that's difficult.
no [nah], + to catch (a person's words) + のが + difficult.

column2: 起きるの早いね。
column3:
You wake up early.
get up + の + early + ね.

column2: 歩くのめんどくさい。
column3:
Walking is such a hassle.
walk + の + bothersome / annoying.

column2: 踊るの楽しい。
column3:
Dancing is fun.
dance + の + fun.

column2: 運転するの難しい。
column3:
Driving is difficult.
drive + の + difficult.

column2: 遊ぶの最高！
column3:
I love partying! // I love hanging out with friends! // I love playing!
play + の + the best.

column2: 食べるの大好き。
column3:
I love eating.
eat + の + loving.

column2: 勉強するの大嫌い。
column3:
I hate studying.
study + の + hating.

column2: 教えるの上手だね。
column3:
You're good at teaching.
teach + の + skilled + だね.
column5: The "you" is understood from context.

column2: 行くのやだなー。
column3:
I don't want to go.
go + の + unpleasant / disliked + だなー.
column5: やだ is a common contraction of 嫌だ（いやだ）, which means, "I don't like that," or "I don't want to do that." It's hard to translate. Also, the なー makes it sound like the speaker is talking to himself or herself.

column2: 出かけるの禁止。
column3:
You can't go out.
go out + の + prohibited.
column5: For example, a parent might say this to a child, or a wife might say it to her husband (or the other way around... if he's brave).

column2: 考えるの疲れる。
column3:
Thinking is tiring. // I'm tired from thinking so much.
think about + の + get tired.

column2: 会うの緊張する。
column3:
I'm nervous to meet her [him]. // I'm nervous about meeting him [her].
meet + の + am nervous.

column2: 今うちにそんな余裕ねーよ!
column3:
We don't have money for that (right now)! // Our family doesn't have money for that (right now)!
now + (our) family + に + that kind of + leeway [surplus; flexibility; room] + do not have + よ!

column2: パパ―、 ハワイ行こうよー！
column3:
Daddy, let's go to Hawaii!
papa [daddy], + Hawaii + let's go + よー!

column3: How many people are in your family?
column5: you = Shiori

column3: I'm resigning from my job for family reasons.

column5: The nuance is that niku-jaga is the quintessential "home cooking food." Niku-jaga, by the way, is a type of Japanese beef stew.

column2: うちは子供5人いるから大変。
column3:
It's tough because there are five kids in my family. // Life is tough because there are five kids in my family.
family + は + child + 5 people + are + because + tough / difficult.

column2: 金持ちのうちに生まれたかった。
column3:
I wish I'd been born into a rich family.
rich + の + family + に + wanted to be born.
column5: Since there is no subjunctive mood in Japanese, we can just say "wanted to" when we want to say "wish I had been" or "would have liked to." If a friend goes to Disneyland but doesn't invite you, later you can say: 行きたかった（いきたかった // I would've liked to go;

column3: I would have liked to have gone, too!

column3: Please leave it to me.

column3:
I don't want to!
I + は + disagreeable + や + わ.
column5: Usually this would be 嫌だ（いやだ）, but (in Kansai dialect), the だ becomes や. Also, わ is a pretty much meaningless sentence-ending particle used by girls. I used to think it was a substitute for よ, but sometimes girls say ～ わよ, so that doesn't make sense.

column2: 日曜日に働くなんて絶対嫌だ。

before + house + am returning + ne

I + の + place/house + let's go + よ.

column3:
Wanna come (over) to my place?
place/house + come?

Let's go to my place [house].
I + んち + let's go + よ.

column3:
Wanna come (over) to my place?
I + んち + come?
column5: Rei said that this phrase, うちんち, is common even for people that don't use うち for "I." It has become a sort of word of its own.

column2: ３つの内１つが正解です。
column3:
One of these three is the correct answer.
three (things) + の + inside + one (thing) + が + correct answer + です.
column5: So, "Inside these 3 things, there is 1 correct answer."

column2: 三つの中一つが正解です。
column3:
One of these three is the correct answer.
three (things) + の + inside + one (thing) + が + correct answer + です.
column5: So, "Inside these 3 things, there is 1 correct answer."

column2: 熱いうちに食べてね。
column3:

hot + inside + に + eat + ね.
column5: In other words, "Eat it before it gets cold!"

column2: 若いうちに勉強しておけばよかった。
column3:

young + うちに + study + if prepared + was good.
column5: You should just memorize ～ ておけばよかった as "I should have ～ (ahead of time)."

column2: ケンタがいないうちに食べちゃおう。
column3:
I think I'll eat this before Kenta gets here! // Let's eat this before Kenta gets here!
Kenta + が + is not (here) + うちに + let's eat (everything).

column3:
I'm gonna party it up while I'm still single!
single + の + うちに + play like crazy!

column2: 今日は食べまくるぞ！
column3: I'm gonna eat a ton today!

healthy + な + うちに + a lot + traveling + let's do.

column3:
I want to get married while I'm still young.
young + うちに + marriage/wedding + want to do.

Let's ask the teacher while she's (still) here. // (I think) I'll ask the teacher while she's (still) here.
teacher + が + is + うちに + ask + let's do (in advance).

mama + が + is not + うちに + playing + に + let's go.

are studying + うちに + skilled + become + よ.

don't know + うちに + was asleep.

column5: Kanto is the region where Tokyo is located. The Kōshin'etsu region encompasses three prefectures: Yamanashi (山梨県), Nagano (長野県), and Niigata (新潟県).

column3: Have you ever been to Nagano?

column3: Where does the Honolulu Marathon start?

column2: 今年の開花日は遅いね。
column3: The cherry blossoms are blooming late this year.

column2: 満開日何日だって？
column3: What day are the cherry blossoms going to be in full bloom?
column5: More literally, "What time is it said that the cherry blossoms are goinh to be in full bloom?"

column2: 満開いつ？
column3:
When will the blossoms be in full bloom?
full bloom + when?

column2: 満開３１日だって。
column3:
Apparently the blossoms will be in full bloom on the 31st. // This says that the blossoms will be in full bloom on the 31st.
full bloom + the 31st + is + って.

column2: 来週お花見しよう！
column3:
Let's go see cherry blossoms next week!
next week + cherry blossom viewing + let's do.
column5: I wanted to say 行こう（いこう // "let's go"）, but Rei said しよう, "let's do" is more common. I'm really off my game today.

column2: 桜綺麗だね。
column3:
(The) Cherry blossoms are pretty, aren't they?
cherry blossoms + pretty + are + ね.
column5: You may have noticed, but you can use kanji or hiragana for 桜／さくら. Rei prefers kanji... as do I.

column2: いい花見スポットありますか。
column3:
Is there a good place to view cherry blossoms (near here)?
good + cherry blossom viewing + spot + is + か.
column5: I thought this was such a strange sentence, because it doesn't have any words like "nearby" or "around here," but Rei didn't think it was necessary. It's little things like this, perhaps, that keep my Japanese from sounding 100% native. Oh, also, since we

column2: 皆様、お話に花の咲いているところではございますが、
column3:
Ladies and gentlemen, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt your conversations, but...
everyone + talk + に + flower + の + is blooming + place + では + is + but.

column2: ここで新婦のお父様、山中ヤスヒロ様より、新婦レナ様へメッセージがございます。
column3:
Now the father of the bride, Mr. Yasuhiro Yamanaka, has a message for his daughter Rena.
here + で + bride + の + father + Yamanaka Yasuhiro-sama + from, + bride + Rena-sama + へ + message + が + has.
column5: より is a fancy way to say "from."

column2: ヤスヒロ様、よろしくお願い致します。
column3:
Please go ahead, Yasuhiro-sama...
Yasuhiro-sama + please
column5: 致します（いたします） is the humble form of します（i.e. する）.

column2: お父さんピアノ弾けるんだ。
column3:
I didn't know your dad played the piano.
dad + piano + can play + んだ.
column5: For a detailed look at this ～ んだ, check out Lesson #46.

column2: やめてよ。
column3: Stop.
column5: This sounds a little feminine, by the way. When speaking strongly like this, a guy would probably say やめろよ, the imperative + よ.

column2: 危ないからやめろよ。
column3: Stop that. It's dangerous!

column2: その曲．．．なんで．．？
column3:
Why did you have to pick that song.
"that + song... + why"
column5: I thought translating this just as "That song... why?" would sound a little strange in English. This is the nuance I got from it.

column2: 下手くそ。
column3:
You suck at this.
extreme clumsiness // very bad (at something)
column5: This is a really common & useful (though rude) word. Let's memorize it!

column2: そこはもっと優しく。
column3:
Play that part softer.
there + は + more + softly
column5: I was tempted to translate this, "You're supposed to play that part softer." I think any English translation will feel overly wordy compared to the Japanese, unfortunately.

column2: 不器用なくせに。
column3:
You know you're no good at this stuff.
clumsy / unskilled + even though
column5: This was the hardest line for me to translate. ～ くせに means something like "even though," but it didn't make sense to me why she would say "even though you're clumsy" here. Asking Rei, her interpretation was that the bride is saying, "Why would you go to a

column2: 頑張ってよ。
column3:
Don't give up.
I hate translating all forms of 頑張る（がんばる // to... persevere? keep at it? not give up? fight? hang in there?）. *_*

column2: 頑張れ。
column3:
Go for it!
You can do this!

column2: 頑張れ．．．お父さん。
column3: Don't give up... Dad.

column2: 音楽は、言葉を超える。
column3:
Music transcends words.
music + は, + words + を + exceeds.
column5: Cool line, yeah?

column2: 自分で学費払ってるの？！偉い！
column3: You're paying the tuition on your own? Good for you!

column2: 中国語で褒め言葉言えるようになりたい。
column3: I want to be able to compliment people in Chinese.

column2: だれか褒めて！（笑）
column3: Someone compliment me! (LOL)

column2: 難しい言葉知ってるね。
column3: You know some difficult words.

column2: かっこいいね。
column3: You look cool. // You're cool.

column2: 靴かっこいいね。
column3:
Cool shoes.
shoes + cool + ね.

column2: かわいいね。
column3: You're (so) cute. // You look cute.

column2: バッグかわいいね。
column3:
Cute bag. // Cute purse.
bag + cute + ね.

column2: センスいいね。
column3: You have good (fashion) sense. // You have a good sense for music. // You have good (musical) sense.

column2: センスあるね。
column3: You have good (fashion) sense.

column2: １０年前の体系に戻したい。
column3: I want to get back to the figure that I had 10 years ago.

column2: スタイルいいね。
column3:
You look good. // You have a nice figure.
style + good + ね.

column2: おしゃれだね。
column3:
You look nice.
smartly dressed / fancy + is + ね.
column5: The nuance of おしゃれ is that someone not only looks nice, but that they look well put together. The person being called おしゃれ is probably wearing nice/expensive clothes. You can also use this word when talking about places, like a "nice/fancy restaurant."

column2: その服似合ってるね。
column3:
Those clothes look good on you.
those + clothes + are suiting + ね.

column2: その服似合ってるよ。
column3:
Those clothes look good on you.
those + clothes + are suiting + よ.

column2: この服似合ってるよね？
column3:
These clothes look good on me, right?
these + clothes + are suiting + よね.

column2: 綺麗だね。
column3:
You're (so) pretty. // You look (so) pretty.
pretty + is + ね.

column2: このコップ欠けてる。
column3: This glass [cup] is chipped.

column2: 草原を駆ける馬の写真を撮った。
column3: I took a picture of a horse running through the open plains.

column2: ほんと？命賭ける？
column3: Really? Would you bet your life on it?

column2: ここに名前書いて。
column3: Write your name here.

column2: ドクロって漢字で書ける？
column3: Can you write the kanji for skull?
column5: I'm guessing that most people are unable to write the ridiculously complicated kanji for "skull," which is 髑髏 (どくろ).

column2: コート掛けようか？
column3:
Want me to hang up your coat?
coat + shall I hang (=かける [volitional form + か])?

column2: ちゃんと布団かけて寝なさい。
column3:
Get under the covers and go to sleep. // Put the covers over you properly and go to sleep.
properly + futon + put on (=かける [te-form]) + sleep (command).
column5: A 布団（ふとん）is not (always) like a futon in English. Rather, it is, in this case, a "comforter," the big fluffy blanket you put on a bed.

column2: ここに水かけて。
column3:
Spray water here. // Rinse off this area.
here + に + water + place (=かける [te-form]).
column5: Sometimes you'll see Japanese people spraying the path or street in front of their houses, especially during summer in order to cool it off (they have lots of water in Japan), which would be appropriate to imagine for this example (maybe two family member

column2: ソースかけるとおいしいよ。
column3:
It's good if you put sauce on it.
sauce + put on (=かける) + と + delicious + よ.

column2: うしろのボタンかけて。
column3:
Button my dress, will you?
back + の + button + fasten (=かける [te-form]).

column2: 鍵かけた？
column3:
Did you lock the door?
lock + put on (=かける [past tense])?

column2: 目覚ましかけて。
column3:
Set the alarm. // Will you set the alarm?
alarm (clock) + put on (=かける [te-form]).
column5: The full word for "alarm clock" is 目覚まし時計（めざましどけい）.

column2: やかんを火にかける。
column3:
Put the kettle on (the stove). // Heat up the kettle.
kettle + を + fire + に + put on (=かける).

column2: 兄に電話をかけた。
column3:
I called my older brother.
older brother + に + phone + を + put on (=かける [past tense]).

column2: 罠にかけて捕まえよう。
column3:
Let's catch him in a trap.
trap + に + hang (=かける [te-form]) + catch / capture.

column2: ネズミに魔法をかけた。
column3:
She put a spell on the rat/mouse.
rat/mouse + に + magic + を + put on (=かける [past tense]).

column2: ブレーキかけて。
column3:
Brake. // Put on the brakes.
brakes + put on (=かける [te-form]).

column2: アイロンかけてくれる？
column3:
Will you iron this for me?
iron + put on (=かける [te-form]) + give me?

column2: 迷惑かけてごめんね。
column3:
I'm sorry for troubling you.
bother/annoyance + put on (=かける [te-form]) + sorry + ね.

column2: お金かけすぎ。
column3:
You spend too much money.
money + かける-too much.
column5: When we attach ～ すぎ（る） to the ます-stem of a verb it means "VERB too much" or "over-VERB." So here we're saying that we "over-put-on money." In other words, spend too much.

column2: 生命保険かけてる。
column3:
I have life insurance.
life insurance + is put on (=かける [present progressive]).

column2: 1分以上会話が続かない人に！ キャバクラで鍛えたコミュニケーション術10選
column3:
For people that can't hold a conversation for more than a minute: 10 communication techniques honed at a hostess club.
one minute + over + conversation + が + won't continue + person + に！
column5: hostess club + で + forged + communication + technique + ten + selection.

column2: 体鍛えてる。
column3:
I'm getting in shape.
body + am forging.

column2: 会話のネタを頭に入れておく。
column3:
Memorize (these) conversation topics.
conversation + の + (joke) material + を + head + に + prepare (~ おく) by inserting (入れて).

column2: アメリカの選挙が話題になっている。
column3: The American elections are a popular topic of conversation right now.

column2: 下ネタ苦手。
column3: I'm not good at talking about dirty topics. // Talking about dirty topics is not my thing.

column2: 会話のネタを語呂にしたものに、適度に整理すべし（テキドニセイリスベシ）という、夜の仕事や営業職の合言葉のようなものがあるので、紹介します。
column3: For night workers and salespersons there is a popular mnemonic for finding conversation material that goes like this: "te-ki-do-ni-se-i-ri-su-be-shi" (= you should moderately organize/arrange).

column2: テレビはよくご覧になりますか？
column3:
Do you watch TV often?
TV + は + often + watch?
column5: ご覧になる（ごらんになる） is a fancy (i.e. very polite) way to say "to see," 見る（みる）.

column2: 暑い日がつづいていますね。
column3:
It's still hot out, isn't it? // It's been hot for a while now, hasn't it?
hot + day + が + are continuing + ね.

column2: 何か趣味はありますか？
column3:
Do you have any hobbies?
something + hobby + は + have?

column2: 駅で火事があったそうです。
column3:
I heard there was a fire at the station. // Apparently there was a fire at the station.
station + で + fire + が + there was + そうです.

column2: お休みの日は何をされていますか？
column3:
What do you do on your days off?
holiday + の + day + は + what + を + are doing (=passive form) + か?

column2: インドに行ったことはありますか？
column3:
Have you ever been to India?
India + に + went + thing + は + there is + か?
column5: Have you ever VERB-ed" in Japanese is ～ たこと（が・は）ありますか, where た is the end of a verb in plain past tense form. Drop the が (or は, depending on tricky particle nuances that you'll pick up slowly over time) and just say ある in casual sentences.

column2: 大物歌手が逮捕されましたね。
column3:
So that famous singer was arrested, right? // That famous singer was arrested.
important person / big shot + singer + が + was arrested + ね.

column2: 大学では何をお勉強されていたんですか？
column3:
What did you study in college?
college + では + what + を + お-studying + was doing (=passive form) + です + か?

column2: 何のお仕事をしていますか？
column3:
What do you do for work?
what + の + お-work + を + are doing + か?

column2: 地球全体の気候が変わってきている。
column3: The climate of the entire earth is changing.

column2: お酒が私の唯一の道楽です。
column3: Alcohol is my one and only hobby.

column2: 大スターといったらマイケル・ジャクソンだよね。
column3: When it comes to naming huge stars, you can't leave out Michael Jackson.
column5: Translating phrases with といったら is really not my thing. Anyways, it means that Michael Jackson is a classic example that comes to mind when thinking of a "huge star."

column2: 最近政治家のスキャンダル多いね。
column3: There have been a lot of scandals about politicians lately, haven't there?

column2: テレビよくみる？
column3:
Do you watch TV often?
TV + often + watch?

column2: 食べてごらん。
column3: Try it.

column2: 食べてみて。
column3: Try it.

column2: 暑い日つづいてるね。
column3:
It's still hot out, isn't it? // It's been hot for a while now, hasn't it?
hot + day + are continuing + ね.

column2: ダイエット続けてる。
column3:
I'm continuing my diet.
diet + am continuing.

column2: ダイエットまだやってる。
column3:
I'm still on my diet. // I'm still dieting.
diet + still + am doing.

column2: なんか趣味ある？
column3:
Do you have any hobbies?
something + hobby + have?

column2: ファッションとか興味ない。
column3: I'm not interested in fashion or anything like that.

column2: 駅で火事があったらしい。
column3:
I heard there was a fire at the station. // Apparently there was a fire at the station.
station + で + fire + が + there was + らしい.

column2: 火貸して。
column3: Can you give me a light?
column5: Used when smoking.

column2: 休みの日何してる？
column3:
What do you do on your days off?
holiday + の + day + は + what + are doing?

column2: 出身どこ？
column3:
Where are you from?
(person's) origin (=city, country, etc.) + where?

column2: インド行ったことある？
column3:
Have you ever been to India?
India + went + thing + there is?

column2: 大物歌手逮捕されたね。
column3:
So that famous singer was arrested, right? // That famous singer was arrested.
important person / big shot + singer + was arrested + ね.

column2: 大学で何勉強してた？
column3:
What did you study in college?
college + で + what + studying + was doing?

column2: 何の仕事してるの？
column3:
What do you do for work?
what + の + work + are doing + の?

column2: 彼女が最近元気ない気がする。
column3:
I have a feeling that she hasn’t been well lately.
She + が + lately + well (energetic) + not + feeling + が + makes.

column2: 家族の為なら何でも出来る気がする。
column3:
I feel like I could do anything for my family.
family + の + sake + if + anything + can do + feeling + が + makes.

column2: 昨日好きな人の前ででっかいクシャミしちゃったわ T_T
column3:
Yesterday I sneezed loudly in front of the guy I like! T_T
yesterday + liked + person + の + in front of + huge + sneeze + did.
column5: This sentence-ending わ is quite feminine-sounding.

column2: 別にいいじゃん、それぐらい。一々気にするな。
column3:
So what? Don’t sweat it so much!
particularly + good + isn't it(?) + that much. + every little thing + don't 気にする (=worry about).
column5: It's worthwhile to just remember 別に（べつに）as "nothing really" or "nothing special," although with いい（じゃん／じゃない？） the meaning becomes "Isn't that fine?" or "That's not such a big deal, is it?" 別にいいじゃん！

column2: …それで鼻水が垂れてさ～、もう最悪！
column3:
…and then my nose was dripping snot. It was the worst!
then + nasal mucus / runny nose + が + droop / drip + さ～, + already + the worst!
column5: This さ～ is kind of like saying "so" or "like."

column2: あ…それやばいな。もう、新しい恋探した方がいいかも。
column3:
Oh, that’s bad. Maybe you should start looking for a new love.
ah + that + dangerous (=slang for "bad; good; cool") + な. + already, + new + love + you should look for + かも (i.e. maybe).

column2: なにそれ 、ひどい！
column3:
That’s just mean!
what + that + cruel / awful / terrible.
column5: なにそれ (what + that) is pretty much a word of its own, meaning "what (the heck is) that?"

column2: 失礼なことして大変申し訳ないです！
column3:
I am very sorry for my rudeness!
rude + thing + do + very / terrible + I'm sorry + です.

column2: いいよ、気にしてないから。
column3:
It’s all right, I don't mind!
good + よ, + 気にしてない + because.
column5: いいよ is a great, casual way to say "It's OK" to someone. Also, ～ してない literally means "am not doing."

column2: 餅を食べる時は気を付けた方がいいよ。のどに詰まりやすいから。
column3:
You should be careful when eating mochi. You can easily choke on it.
mochi + eat + when + は + careful + better + よ. Throat + in + get stuck + easily + because.

column2: 気のせいか。
column3: Guess it was just my imagination.

column2: 私助手席乗っていい？
column3:
Mind if I sit in the front? // Is it OK if I sit in the front?
I + passenger seat + ride (て-form) + good?
column5: The verb 乗る（のる）, while technically meaning "to get on; to board," can also mean "to ride." It has like a million meanings, actually.

column2: 俺助手席乗る！
column3:
I call front seat! // I'm gonna sit in the front!
I + passenger seat + ride!
column5: I chose 俺（おれ）this time for "I," but just to show we can use lots of different words for "I." Also, because I never say 私（わたし）. I say 俺（おれ） with friends and close family (i.e. 90% of my conversations) and 僕（ぼく） when I'm trying to be polite (i.e. in polite

column2: 僕がやります。
column3: I'll do it.

column2: あたし助手席。
column3:
I call front seat. // I'm in the front.
I + passenger seat.
column5: あたし is only for girls. You can use it in casual sentences.

column2: 私前乗っていい？
column3:
Mind if I sit in the front? // Is it OK if I sit in the front?
I + front/before + ride (て-form) + good?

column2: 俺前乗る！
column3:
I call front seat! // I'm gonna sit in the front!
I + front/before + ride!

column2: あたし前。
column3:
I call front seat. // I'm in the front.
I + front/before.
column5: Since we don't have a verb like 乗る（のる） or a clear and specific word like 助手席（じょしゅせき）, this sentence is highly dependent on context. It must be painfully obvious to the listener that the "front" you're referring to is the front of the car. In such a case,

column2: うちの親、できちゃった婚だよ。
column3: My parents got married because my mom was pregnant.

column2: まさか自分が出来婚するとは。
column3: I can't believe I'm getting married because I got knocked up.
column5: When speaking in English, we'd put emphasis on the word "I'm" to stress that I can't believe that I, of all people, am getting married because I'm pregnant. The Japanese shares this nuance using the words まさか and とは (to wa).

column2: 料理出来るよ。
column3:
I can cook.
cooking + can do + よ.
column5: Here, よ is adding emphasis and has the nuance that the speaker is either defending their ability to cook or maybe showing off a bit.

column2: 上手に出来た！
column3:
It turned out great!
skillfully + was able to do/make.
column5: We would know that the speaker is talking about, for example, the cake that they made... because it's probably sitting right in front of them when they say this.

column2: 子供出来た。
column3:
I'm pregnant.
child + was able to make.

column2: 子供産んだ。
column3:
I had a baby.
child + gave birth.

column2: 子供生まれた。
column3:
I had a baby.
child + was born.
column5: The speaker could be the mother or the father.

column2: 財布忘れてしまいました。
column3:
I forgot my wallet.
wallet + forget (て-form) + did completely.

column2: 財布忘れてしまった。
column3:
I forgot my wallet.
wallet + forget (て-form) + did completely.

column2: 財布忘れちゃった。
column3:
I forgot my wallet.
wallet + forgot (oops).
column5: ～てしまう, in casual sentences, gets shortened to ～ちゃう, and in past tense that's ～ちゃった.

column2: 結婚しよう！
column3: Let's get married!

column2: 婚約しました。
column3: I got engaged.

column2: 家族の笑顔が私の元気の元です。
column3: My family's smiling faces are the source of my energy.
column5: "Energy" is not the best word for 元気 here... but there's not really ever a best word for 元気.

column2: 元旦は実家？
column3: Are you going to spend New Year's Day at your parents' house?

column2: 元日に開いてるスーパー知ってる？

hair + long + ね.

how much + の + size?

thick + book + って + read + の + tough/difficult.

this + steak, + amazing + thickness.

heavy + thing + carry + の + help + give me?

price + は + weight + according to + changes.

this + book + difficult.

English + and + Japanese + の + difficulty + って + which + が + above + かな？

deep + place + until + don't go + ね.

sea/ocean + の + depth + って + can't imagine + よね.

It's cold today.
today + cold + ね.

winter + の + coldness + poor (at).

I want to live in a big house.
wide + house + に + want to live.

What size place are you looking for?
spaciousness (=wideness) + は + how much + が + good + is + か？

Vegetables are good for you.
vegetables + は + body + に + good.

column3:
I don't get what's so great about smartphones.
smartphone + の + merit / good quality + が + not at all + don't understand.

When you're tall, many troublesome things happen.
Tall + if/and + various + be troubled + right?

column2: あー、分かる分かる。色んな所に頭ぶつけるよね。
column3:
Oh, I know I know. You bang your head into a lot of places. right?
Oh + understand + understand. + various + places + に + head + bang + right?

Want some chocolate?
chocolate + eat?

I'm on a diet...
Diet + in the middle of + です...

Oh, I see.
Oh, + that (is how it) is + だ
column5: there is not much difference between あー and ああ, except that あー is usually 'flat' in tone (no change in the pitch of the voice when pronounced), and ああ can have a little variation, you can start with a note and then lower or raise it. It's hard to convey t

column2: うんうん 。
column3:
Yeah, I know what you mean'
yeah yeah
column5: Used when you can relate to what the person is saying, or when you completely understand what they mean or agree with it.

column2: 痩せようと思ってスポーツ始めたら今度は筋肉が増えちゃってさあ～
column3:
(I was) thinking of losing weight so I started doing sports, but then my muscle mass increased...
get thinner + と + thought(-te form) + sports + started (-tara form -- expresses 'and then') + this time + は + muscles + increased (-te form) + さあ～

column2: うんうん、やっぱり。
column3:
Oh, yes, (I know)
Yeah Yeah + as I thought.

column2: 結局痩せられなかった。
column3:
In the end I couldn't lose weight/ didn't get thinner.
Finally + couldn't get thinner.

column2: 私もそうなんだよね。
column3:
It was the same for me, you know?
Me + also + like this + だ + よ + ね.

column2: ねえ、起きてる？
column3: Hey, are you awake?

column2: お弁当は自分で作ってるの？
column3: Do you make (your) bentos yourself?

column2: ううん、お母さんが作ってる。
column3: No, mom makes them.

column2: へえ～。
column3:
Oh, is that so?
Used when you are surprised, when the speaker said something (mildly) unexpected or something that didn’t cross your mind or when you find something out.

column2: ねえ、ミルクセーキ飲む？
column3:
Hey, do you want a milkshake?
Hey, + milkshake + drink?

column2: ううん、実は牛乳飲めないの。
column3:
Nah, I actually can't drink milk.
Uh-uh, the truth is + milk + can't drink + の.
column5: This の at the end of the sentence sounds feminine. With the exception of questions, の always sounds feminine at the end of sentences.

column2: へえ、知らなかった。
column3:
Heee, I didn't know that.
へえ, + didn't know.

column2: えっ？
column3: Huh?
column5: This is used when the other person does or says something (very) surprising, especially when this puts you or someone else in a troublesome situation.

column2: ねえ、付き合ってくれない？
column3:
Hey, wanna go out?
Hey, + will you go along with me / go out with me / keep me company?
column5: It could sound like this speaker wants to date the listener.

column2: コンビニまで！
column3:
To the convenience store!
convenience store + until.

column2: ああ、うん！
column3: Oh, yeah!

column2: 仕事は辛いけど皆で一緒に頑張ってると楽しい。
column3:
Work is hard, but if we all do our best together, it’s fun.
Work + は + difficult + but + everyone + で (with) + together + do one’s best + と + fun.

column2: 最近天気よくないね？
column3:
The weather was bad lately, ne?
Lately + weather + not good + ne?

column2: 今週末どこか遊び行かない？
column3:
Wanna go have fun somewhere this weekend?
This weekend + somewhere + play + go?

column2: そうだね、行こう行こう！
column3:
Yeah, let’s go, let’s go!
You’re right, aren’t you? + Let’s go + let’s go!

column2: 腕相撲しよう！
column3:
Let’s do arm wrestling!
arm-sumo + let's do.

column2: いいよ、しようしよう！
column3:
All right, let’s do, let’s do!
sure + let's do + let's do.

column2: 私人が多い所苦手なんです。
column3:
I don't like crowded places.
I + people + が + many + place + poor (at) + なん(short for 'なの') です.
column5: So "I'm not good at places where there are many people (around)." なの is also used in sentences to make an assertion, but only in female language.

column2: そうなんですか？知りませんでした。
column3:
Really? I didn’t know that.
is that so? + didn't know.

column2: そっか。
column3: Oh. // I see.
column5: Basically the less polite version of そうですか.

column2: ごめん、用事が出来て飲み会行けなくなった。
column3:
Sorry, something came up and I can’t come for drinks.
Sorry + errand + が + to do + drinking party + cannot go + became.

column2: そっか。じゃあ、また今度だね。
column3:
Really? Well, next time it is then.
Really? + Well, + again + this time / next time + is + ね.
column5: In 用事が出来た(ようじ が できる) we see another use for this infamous できる verb. It means that you ‘sorta managed’ to 'make' an errand. This way of expressing it gives off a more passive role to the speaker. So they are letting you know that they didn’t actively seek

column2: 子供ができたみたい。
column3: I think I'm pregnant.
column5: The speaker might, for example, be informing her husband that she's pregnant.

column2: 仰る通りです。
column3:
I completely agree with you.
(It is) as you say.
column5: 仰る is the honorific language version of 話す （はなす） to speak.

column2: 仕事が増えたから残業しなきゃな。
column3:
(We) have more work, so (we) must work overtime.
Work + が + increased + because + overtime + must do.

column2: お世話になっております。Nikoです。
column3:
Greetings. This is Niko.
assistance + に + is becoming. + Niko + is.
column5: There is no good translation for お世話になっております. Technically, it means something like "I am humbly receiving your aid," and sometimes it will even be translated as, "It's a pleasure working with you." If you look at this article, he just uses, "Hey, how's it

column2: レコーディングの件ですが、その後進捗はいかがでしょうか。
column3:
How is everything going with those recordings? // About those recordings, how is everything going since (the) last time (we talked)?
recording + の + matter/case + is + but, + that + after + progress + は + how + でしょうか.

column2: 子供は進歩がはやいね。
column3: Children develop quickly, huh?

column2: 4月14日にお送りいただけるとのことでしたので、そろそろ音声データをお送りいただけると助かるのですが。
column3:
You mentioned that I would be able to receive the recordings on 04/14. If you could send them soon, it would really be a huge help to me.
April 14th + に + sending + could receive + とのことでした (=was the thing/agreement) + because, + soon + voice recording + data + を + sending + could receive + if/and + be saved + の + is + が.

column2: 現状をお知らせいただけますと幸いです。
column3:
If you could let me know where things are at, it would really mean a lot to me.
present condition + を + notification + can receive + if/and + happy/happiness + is.

column2: [Something] をいただけると幸いです。
column3: If I could get [something] from you, it would mean a lot to me. // If you could get [something] for me, I would really appreciate it.

column2: どうぞよろしくお願いいたします。
column3:
Thank you. // I look forward to hearing from you. // Thank you for your time.
Yeah, there is no good translation for language like this. Just memorize it! Oh, also, note that いたします is the humble form of します, so this is more polite than saying お願いします.

column2: 黒い靴欲しい。
column3:
I want (some) black shoes.
black + shoes + wanted.

column2: 見て、白い猫がいる。
column3:
Look, there's a white cat.
look, + white + cat + が + is.

column2: 酔ってるでしょ？顔赤いよ。

column3: Blue cake?! Gross!

column2: 一番好きな色は何ですか。
column3:
What is your favorite color?
number one + liked + color + は + what + is + か.

column2: 一番好きな色はなに？
column3:
What's your favorite color?
number one + liked + color + は + what?
column5: I put 何 in hiragana here, as なに, because I saw that much more in casual sentences online. Both ways should be fine, though.

column2: 黒（が一番好き）。
column3:
Black (is my favorite).
black + (が + number one + liked).

column2: 黒と白どっちがすき？
column3:
Which do you like better, black or white?
black + and + white + which + が + liking?

column2: 赤と青をまぜると紫になる。
column3:
If/When you mix red and blue, you get purple.
red + and + blue + を + mix + and + purple + becomes.

column2: 緑を守ろう。
column3: Let's protect the environment.
column5: More literally, "Let's protect green."

column2: あの緑色の机はいくらですか？
column3: How much is that green desk?

column2: 茶色いソファ買おうかな。
column3:
Maybe I should buy a brown sofa.
brown + sofa + let's buy + かな.
column5: If you're confused by this use of "volitional verb + かな," then you should check out Lessons #54 and #55.

column2: 茶色のシャツ持ってる？

brown + の + shirt + are possessing/holding?

column2: この花、きれいな紫色だね。
column3:
This flower is a beautiful violet (color).
this + flower, + pretty + violet + is + ね.

column2: 髪の黒さを自慢する。

She is proud of how black her hair is.
hair + の + blackness + を + boasts/is proud of.

column2: 歯の白さが素敵。
column3:
She has such wonderful white teeth.
teeth + の + whiteness + が + lovely.
column5: This word 素敵 always sounds feminine to me. I guess that's somewhat true of the word "lovely," too?

column2: 目の茶色さは人によって違う。
column3:
Different people's eyes are different shades of brown. // The shade of brown of people's eyes depends on the person.
eye + の + brown-ness + は + person + depending on + differs.
column5: You should definitely memorize "X + によって違う," which we can think of as "It depends on the X."

column2: おどろきの白さに！
column3:
Look at how white it's gotten!
surprise + の + whiteness + に！
column5: This is a phrase you might hear in a TV commercial about laundry detergent or bleach, for example.

column2: 正しい敬語を使っている人はとても少ない。
column3: There are very few people that use honorific language correctly.
column5: I was a bit torn about how to translate 敬語 (けいご). "Honorific language" is good, I suppose. But it could also just mean "(very) polite language." The specific term for "honorific language" is 尊敬語 (そんけいご), which is used when raising the status of the person

column2: 次の文を謙譲語を使った文に直しなさい。

column5: For example, this phrase could show up on a test.

column2: 「なさる」は「する」の尊敬語です。
column3: "Nasaru" is the honorific form of "suru."

column2: 私はライアン・ゴズリングと申します。
column3:
I am Ryan Gosling.
I + は + name + am called

column2: 私はライアン・ゴズリングです。
column3: I am Ryan Gosling.

I came in April of last year.
last year + の + April + に + came

column3: I came in April of this year.

I saw the document yesterday.
yesterday + that + document + を + saw

column3: I saw the document yesterday.

column2: 明日お宅へ参ります。
column3: Tomorrow I will go to your house.
column5: 参ります (まいります) is the humble form of both 行きます (いきます) and 来ます (きます).

column2: 母は家におります。
column3: My mother is at home.
column5: おります is the humble form of います, "to be."

column2: 先日は立派なケーキをありがとうございます。家族でおいしく頂きました。
column3: Thank you for that wonderful cake the other day. My family and I really enjoyed it.
column5: In this case, 頂く (いただく) is the humble form of 食べる (たべる), "to eat."

column2: 明日の午前中に伺います。
column3: I will go there tomorrow morning.
column5: In this case, 伺う (うかがう) is a humble verb meaning "to visit."

column2: お酒も少しは頂きます。
column3: I also drink alcohol a little bit.
column5: Here, 頂く (いただく) is a humble verb meaning "to drink."

column2: お目にかかれて光栄です。
column3: It's an honor to meet you.
column5: お目にかかる (おめにかかる) is a humble way of saying "to meet."

column2: 今日中にご連絡いたします。
column3: I will contact you sometime today.
column5: Adding the ご to 連絡 (れんらく) makes it more formal. Also, いたします is the humble form of します.

column2: プロジェクトのことは存じております。
column3: I know about the project.
column5: 存じております (ぞんじております) is the humble form of 知っています (しっています), "to know (of/about)."

column2: お礼にこの花を差し上げます。
column3: To show my gratitude, I'd like to offer you these flowers.
column5: 差し上げる (さしあげる) is the humble form of あげる, "to give."

column2: 社長からワインを頂きました。
column3: I received a bottle of wine from the (company) president.
column5: In this case, 頂く (いただく) is the humble form of もらう, "to receive."

column2: 荷物をお持ちしましょうか？
column3:
May I carry your bags for you?
bags (luggage) + を + carry + か

column2: 荷物を持ちましょうか？
column3: Shall I carry your luggage?

column2: ご連絡お待ちしております。
column3:
I look forward to hearing from you.
ご+ contact + waiting

column2: どうぞ、食べてください。
column3: Please go ahead and eat.

column2: そのメールをご覧になりましたか？
column3:
Did you see that e-mail?
that + e-mail + を + see + か

column2: そのメールを見ましたか。
column3: Did you see that e-mail?

column2: ジョンさんのことはご存じですか？
column3:
Do you know John?
John + の + thing + は + know + か

column2: ジョンさんのことは知っていますか?
column3: Do you know John?

column2: 明日はどこにいらっしゃるのですか？
column3: Where will you go tomorrow?
column5: Here, いらっしゃる is the honorific form of "to go."

column2: もうすぐ社長がいらっしゃいます。
column3: The (company) president will be arriving soon.
column5: Here, いらっしゃる is the honorific form of "to come."

column2: 三浦さんはいらっしゃいますか？
column3: Is Miura-san available?
column5: Here, いらっしゃる is the humble form of "to be."

column2: どんなお酒を召し上がりますか？
column3: What type of alcohol do you like to drink?
column5: Here, 召し上がる (めしあがる) is the honorific form of "to drink."

column2: 先生がそうおっしゃいました。
column3: That's what my teacher said.
column5: おっしゃる is the honorific form of 言う (いう), "to say."

column2: パンとライス、どちらになさいますか？
column3: Would you like bread or rice?
column5: Remember that なさる is the honorific form of する. Here it means "choose."

column2: 高価な時計をくださいました。
column3: He [She] gave me an expensive watch.
column5: くださる is the honorific form of くれる, meaning "to give (when the giver is someone other than the speaker, or someone further from the speaker psychologically than the person receiving the gift)."

column2: 小説はお読みになりますか？
column3: Do you read novels?
column5: Here the verb 読む (よむ), "to read" is being made into an honorific form.

column2: お聞きになりましたか ？
column3:
Did you hear (about what happened)?
hear + か

column2: 聞きましたか？
column3: Did you hear (about what happened)?

column2: 聞いた？
column3: Did you hear (about what happened)?

column2: どうぞお入り(になって)ください。
column3:
Please, come in.
go ahead + enter + please

column2: どうぞ入ってください。
column3: Please, come in.

column2: 丁寧語は簡単だね。
column3: Polite language is easy, huh?

column2: まもなく東京駅に到着いたします。
column3:
Soon, we will be arriving at Tokyo Station.
soon + Tokyo + station + に + arrive + to do

column2: もうすぐ、東京駅に到着します。
column3: Soon, we will be arriving at Tokyo Station.

column2: 申し訳ありませんが、本日は臨時休業いたします。
column3:
We apologize, but we are closed for today.
sorry + が + today + は + special holiday + do

column2: ごめんなさい、今日は臨時休業です。
column3: I'm sorry, but we are closed today.

column2: こちらのテーブルでよろしいでしょうか？
column3: Is this table all right?
column5: This sentence would, for example, be said by a waiter showing restaurant guests to their table. よろしいでしょうか is a much softer and more polite way of saying いいですか.

column2: 外国の方ですか？
column3: Are you a foreigner?
column5: 方 (かた) is a polite way to say 人 (ひと), "person." So literally this sentence means, "Are you a foreign country person?" Spend enough time in Japan, and I can almost guarantee you'll hear a Japanese person say the words "foreign country person" in English.

column2: 受付は２階でございます。
column3: The reception desk is on the second floor.
column5: でございます is a polite form of です.

column2: お水四つください。
column3: Four waters, please.

column2: ご質問がありましたら、遠慮なく私へご連絡下さい。
column3:
If you have any question, please don’t hesitate and contact me.
question + が + have + if + hesitate + なく + me + へ + contact + please

column2: どうぞごゆっくりお召し上がり くださいませ。
column3:
Please take your time to eat.
go head + slowly + eat + please
column5: ませ is used as the imperative here. As in いらっしゃいませ, it is politely asking you to do an action.

column2: JR線は、お乗り換えください。
column3:
Please transfer to the JR line.
JR + line + transfer + please

column2: お茶いる？
column3: Do you want some tea?

column2: お客様、お待たせいたしました。
column3: I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.
column5: You'll hear お待たせいたしました frequently in Japan. This sentence literally means "(Honorable) Customer, I (humbly) made you wait." The sentence following this example could be something like, "Your table is ready now" or "Please follow me."

column2: ご案内します。
column3: I'll show you to your table [to your seats, etc.].
column5: This is very polite language. More literally, the sentence means "I'll guide you."

column2: お箸つけますか？
column3: Would you like chopsticks?
column5: For example, if you buy a bento [boxed lunch] at a convenience store, they might ask you this.

column2: まもなく京都、京都駅に到着いたします。
column3: Soon, the train will arrive in Kyoto, Kyoto station.

column2: この電車のお手洗いは２号車にございます。
column3: The restroom is in car number 2 on this train.

column2: お弁当、サンドイッチ、お飲み物などをご用意して、係員がお席まで伺います。
column3: Boxed meals, sandwiches and beverages are available. The salesperson will come by your seat.

column2: OLやめたい！
column3: I want to quit working as an OL!

column2: もしもし、XX会社です。
column3:
Hello, XX Company.
hello + XX company + です

column2: Customer Name です。Boss Name様はいらっしゃいますか。
column3:
This is Customer Name. Is Boss Name there?
Customer Name + です。+ Boss Name +honorific ending + there + か

column5: This sounds like the speaker is talking to a police officer investigating some sort of crime... or perhaps making a call to the police.

column2: たしかに受け取りました。

I acknowledge the receipt of this item.
certainly + received.

column2: たしかに安いけど、それでも欲しくない。
column3:
Yeah, it's definitely cheap, but I still don't want it.
certainly + cheap + but + nevertheless / even so + is not wanted.

column2: このレストラン値段の割に微妙じゃない？
column3:
This restaurant doesn't quit live up to its prices, does it?
this + restaurant + price + の + comparatively / in proportion + doubtful / questionable + is not?
column5: 割に and 微妙 are both extremely common words, and I highly recommend memorizing both. Saying that something is 微妙 is never really a good thing. In this case, the restaurant is 微妙（びみょう / doubtful; not quite right）in comparison to（割に《わりに》）the price.

column2: これはたしか渋谷で買ったと思う。

column5: "This" is probably a piece of clothing or a bag. The listener probably asked where the speaker got it.

those + two people, + if I'm not mistaken + last year + marriage / wedding + did + はず + is + よ.

What time does the (drinking) party start, again?
drinking party + what time + from + is + っけ？

column2: たしか6時から。

cat tongue?

Can I get that without celery?
celery + omit + can I receive?
column5: Feel free to replace セロリ with whatever food you want left out of your order.

Ladder + に + climbed (verb with て form) + above + from + garden + を + looked.

column5: In Japanese the verb '鳴く/なく' is used to express that an animal is making a sound, be that a 'chirp,' a 'meow,' a 'woof,' or whatever. Also, this verb is a homonym with 'to cry' （泣く/なく）. So you have:

column2: 蛙が鳴いている。
column3:
The frog is croaking.
Frog + が + croaking

column2: 子供が泣いている。
column3:
The child is crying.
Child + が + crying

column2: ひよこが孵る。
column3:
The chicks hatch.
Chicks + が + to hatch

column2: 花が咲く。
column3:
The flowers bloom.
Flowers + が + to bloom.

column2: 花が散る。
column3:
The leaves fall.
Leaves + が + fall
column5: The verb '散る' tends to only be used with flowers and leaves that fall/scatter. If, for example, a book happens to fall down, you use the well-known '落ちる/おちる/to fall', so make sure not to mix them up.

column2: 天井から何かが落ちた。
column3: Something fell from the ceiling.

column2: 曇ってる。
column3:
It's cloudy.
is being cloudy.
column5: It's common to remove the い from 曇っている in spoken language.

column2: 晴れてる。
column3:
It's clear out.
is being clear
column5: It's common to remove the い from 晴れている in spoken language.

column2: 日が暮れる。
column3:
The sun sets.
Sun + が + to set

column2: 日が沈む。
column3:
The sun sets.
Sun + が + to sink

column2: 食べかけのりんご。
column3:
A partially eaten apple.
Eat (masu-stem) + かけ + の + apple.

column2: 作りかけの料理。
column3:
A partially cooked food.
Make (masu-stem) + かけ + の + food
column5: This does not refer to uncooked food - like insufficiently cooked, but to the case where somebody started making it and left while in the middle of it.

column2: 電話を掛ける。
column3:
To make a phone call.
Phone + を + make/call

column2: 声を掛ける。
column3:
To start a conversation.
Voice + を + call

column2: 壁に絵を掛ける。
column3:
To hang a painting on a wall.
wall + に + picture + を + hang

column2: 腰かける。
column3:
To sit down.
Hips + sit.
column5: This phrase shows up in dictionaries as a single verb entry. So feel free to ignore the literal translation, if you'd like.

column2: どうぞおかけになって下さい。
column3:
Please have a seat.
By all means + sit + に + become + please
column5: You must have noticed the 'お' in front of 'かけ' which is just our well known politeness prefix, as also seen in 'お金/おかね/money' or 'お休み/おやすみ/rest'.

column2: 今月お金ない。
column3: I don't have money this month.

column2: お休みはいつですか？
column3: When are your days off?

column2: 命を懸ける。
column3:
To risk one's life.
Life + を + put at stake
column5: The nuance here is "to put one's life on the line" when trying to do something. With a different kanji, 命を賭ける (いのちをかける) means "to bet one's life."

column2: 鍵を掛ける。
column3:
To lock.
key + を + lock

column2: 迷惑をかける。
column3:
To bother (someone).
Bother/burden + を + かける(error 404: literal translation not found)

column2: エンジンをかける。
column3:
To start an engine.
Engine + を + activate/turn on

column2: 音楽をかける。
column3:
To play music.
Music + を + play

column2: 2かける2は4です。
column3:
2 times 2 is 4.
2 + multiply + 2 + は + 4 + です.

column2: そんな格好して出かけるの？ほとんど裸じゃない！
column3:
Are you going out looking like this? You're basically naked!
that kind (of) + appearance + make + go out + の? + Mostly + naked + right?
column5: 格好（かっこう） has the general meaning of 'appearance', and it can be used to refer to the way that someone dresses, but also to the general 'vibe' a person gives off.

column2: 格好いい。
column3:
Cool.
Appearace + good
column5: By itself, technically 格好 is かっこう, but when it combines with いい, we drop the う, giving us: かっこいい.

column2: いつかすっぽんぽんで海泳いでみたい！
column3: Someday I'd like to swim in the ocean completely naked!

column2: ドレスを着る。
column3:
To wear a dress.
Dress + を + wear

column2: スーツを着る。
column3:
To wear a suit.
Suit + を + wear

column2: 上着を着る。
column3:
To wear a coat.
Coat/jacket + を + wear
column5: 上着 can refer to any type of outerwear.

column2: ズボンを履く。
column3:
To put on/wear pants.
Pants + を + put on/wear

column2: 靴を履く。
column3:
To put on/wear shoes.
Shoes + を + put on/wear

column2: 靴下を履く。
column3:
To put on/wear socks.
Socks + を + put on/wear

column2: 眼鏡を掛ける。
column3:
To put glasses on.
To put on/wear glasses.
Glasses + を + put on/wear.
column5: You may or may not know that the word 'to put on' in Japanese changes depending on what it is that you put on.

column2: 帽子を被る。
column3:
To wear/put on a hat.
Hat + を + put on/wear

column2: 猫を被る。
column3:
To feign friendliness.
Cat + を + wear/put on

column2: 気になりませんよ。
column3: I'm not worried about it. / I wouldn't worry about it.

column2: 以下、気になった点。
column3:
Some of concerns are listed below.
below + keep in mind + points

column2: 隣の音が気になる。
column3:
I am worried about the noise next door.
next door + の + noise + が + worry

column2: 少し気になりました。
column3:
I was a little worried.
a little + worried

column2: マリオの彼女がどんな人か気になる！
column3:
I wonder what Mario's girlfriend is like.
Mario + の + girlfriend + が + what kind of + person + か + (I'm) curious!

column2: わかる気がします。
column3:
I think I might understand.
understand + have a feeling

column2: 勝てる気がする。
column3:
I think we can win.
can win + feel

column2: 自然な気がします。
column3:
Seems natural.
natural + な + feeling

column2: 気をつけて！
column3: Watch out!

column2: 熱いから気をつけてね。
column3:
Be careful, it's hot.
hot + because + be careful + ね

column2: 今後気をつけます。
column3:
From now on, I will pay attention.
from now on + pay attention

column2: 気をつけよう。
column3:
Let’s be careful.
let’s be careful

column2: 足もとに気をつけてください。
column3:
Watch your step.
step + に + watch out + please

column2: 日本は気に入った？
column3:
Do you like Japan?
Japan + は + like

column2: なに、気に入らん？
column3:
What, you don’t like it?
​what, + don't like?
column5: I wouldn't recommend using this exact phrase... unless you're an older man in an anime or something. The speaker sounds a bit angry.

column2: 一目で気に入った。
column3:
I liked it at a glance.
at first glance + で + pleased with.

column2: 大変気に入りました。
column3:
We really like it.
greatly + pleased

column2: 参加する気はあるの？
column3:
You interested in participating?
participate + do + interested + の
column5: The speaker sounds just a little angry.

column2: 全く働く気がありません。
column3:
I have no inclination to work.
none + work + interest

column2: 彼女も俺に気があるみたい。
column3:
I think she's into me, too.
her + also + I + に + feel inclined + looks like.

column2: 途中で忘れものに気が付いた。
column3:
I realized that I'd forgotten something while on my way there.
on the way + で + forgotten thing + に + noticed

column2: 全然気が付かなかった。
column3:
I didn’t notice it at all.
at all + didn’t notice

column2: 髪切ったの気付いた？
column3: Did you notice that I got my hair cut?

column2: あたしのこと愛してる？
column3: Do you love me?

column2: 俺ヒップホップ大好きなんだ。
column3: I love hip hop.

column2: "子どもの頃の話。"
column3:
A story from my childhood.
child + の + time + の + story
column5: 頃 means “at that approximate time,” and it usually used in a set phrase as 子どもの頃 like above to mean “when I was a child.”

column2: "子どもの頃、僕は２階建ての借家にすんでいた。 "
column3:
When I was a child I lived in a rented 2 story house.
child + の + time + I + は + 2 story + の + rented house + に + lived
column5: ～階建て is a counter for “n-story house.”

column2: "母親も仕事をしていたので、学校から帰っても自分一人のことが多かった。 "
column3:
Since my mother also worked, I was often home by myself after school.
mother + also + work + を + did + since + school + from + return home + も + self + alone + の + こと + が + often

column2: 母は10年前に亡くなりました。
column3: My mother passed away ten years ago.

column2: ジャックのお母さんってどんな人？
column3: What's your mom like?
column5: ジャック = Jack = you

column2: "ある日、夕方遅く学校から帰ってくると、家の中が暗い。"
column3:
One day, when I came home from school late in the evening, the house was dark.
one day + evening + late + school + from + return home + come + と + house + の + inside +が + dark

column2: "「おかあさ～ん」と呼ぶと、２階から小さな声で「はあ～い」と 応える声がする。"
column3:
When I yelled “Mom,” I heard a small voice answer “yes,” from the second floor.
mom + と + call + と + 2nd floor + from + small + voice + で + “yes” + と + answer + voice + が + する
column5: The ～ symbol in this case means an elongation of the word when you are speaking. So はあ～い, is much like the English “yeeeees.”

column2: もういっかい呼ぶとまた「はあ～い」。
column3:
When I called again, again I heard “yes.”
one more time + call + と + again + yes

column2: "自分を呼んでいるような気がして、２階へあがる。 "
column3:
It felt like it was calling out to me, so I climb to the 2nd floor.
self + を + calling + like + feeling + 2nd floor + へ + climb.

column2: "階段をあがったところでまた母親を呼ぶと、奥の部屋から「はあ～い」と声がする。 "
column3:
As I was climbing the stairs, when I called my mother again, from the inside room, the voice said “yes.”
stairs + を + climb + ところで + again + mother + を + call + と + interior + room + from + “yes” + と + voice + が + do

column2: "奇妙な胸騒ぎを感じるのと、いっこくも早く母に会いたいのとで、奥の部屋へゆっくりと 近づいていく。 "
column3:
I slowly moved closer to the inside room because I had a strange premonition and I wanted to see my mother.
strange + premonition + を + feel + のと + right away + mother + に + want to see + のと + で + inside + の + room + へ + slowly + と + got closer.
column5: ～のと～のと in this sentence is showing the reason for doing something. The narrator climbs up the stairs because he has a strange premonition and he wants to see his mother, のと is just labeling those reasons.

column2: "そのとき、下で玄関を開ける音がする。"
column3:
In that moment, there was the noise of the front door opening below me.
in that moment + below + で + entryway + を + open + sound + が + do
column5: 玄関 is the small entrance space in which you remove your shoes in a Japanese house, after entering the front door. Even the smallest apartments have one.

column2: "母親があわただしく買い物袋をさげて帰ってきた。"
column3:
My mother hurriedly came in, the shopping bags hanging from her.
mother + が + hurriedly + shopping bag + を + to hang from + return home + came

column2: "「しゅんすけ、帰ってる～？」明るい声で僕を呼んでいる。 "
column3:
“Shunsuke, are you home?” Her bright voice was calling me.
“Shunsuke + return home + bright + voice + で + me + を + calling”
column5: 帰ってる in this sentence in “the state of returning home.” So even though it is not past tense, she is asking if Shunsuke is currently at home.

column2: "僕はすっかり元気を取り戻して、階段を駆け下りていく。 "
column3:
I regained my composure and ran down the stairs.
I + は + thoroughly + vigor + を + take back + stairs + を + rundown + go

column2: "そのとき、ふと奥の部屋に目をやる。"
column3:
In that moment, I look toward the inside room.
in that moment + without reason + inside + の + room + に + look toward

column2: "奥の部屋のドアがキキキとわずかに動いた。 "
column3:
The door to the inside room creaked, moving a little.
inside + の + room + の + door + が + creak + と + a little + moved
column5: キキキ is an onomatopoeia that the door makes as it is creaking open.

column2: "僕は一瞬、ドアのすきまに奇妙なものを見た。 "
column3:
For a moment, I saw something strange through the crack in the door.
I + は + one moment + door + の + gap, crack + に + strange + thing + saw

column2: "こっちを見ている白い人間の顔だった。"
column3:
It was the white face of a person looking.
here + を + looking + white + person + の + face + だった

column2: やっと終わった！
column3:
I've finally finished! // It's finally over!
at last + finished.

column2: なにが？
column3:
With what? // What is? // About what?
what + が？
column5: Like I've said before, が is the "pointer particle." And by saying it after なに, "what," the speaker is asking the listener to "point" to "what" they are talking about.

column2: なにが終わったの？
column3: What is finished?

column2: はやくやらなきゃ。
column3:
I have to do it soon.
soon / quickly + have to do.

column2: なにを？
column3:
Do what?
what + を？

column2: なにをやらなきゃ？
column3: You have to do what?

column2: もうすぐ誕生日だ。
column3:
It's almost her [his] birthday.
very soon + birthday + だ.

column2: 誰の？
column3:
Whose birthday?
who + の？

column2: 誰の誕生日？
column3: Whose birthday?

column2: 手紙書くんだ。
column3:
I'm going to write a letter.
letter + write + んだ.

column2: 誰に？
column3:
To who?
who + に？

column2: 誰に手紙を書くの？
column3: Who are you going to write a letter to?

column2: 行ってくる！
column3:
I'll go there real quick.
go (te-form) + come!
column5: A semi-literal translation of this sentence would be "I'll go and come back," but that sounds a little stiff in English. You can use 行ってくる if you're going to go somewhere and come back relatively quickly.

column2: どこに？
column3:
Go where?
where + に？

column2: どこに行くの？
column3: Where are you going?

column2: お母さんはどうする？
column3:
What are you gonna, Mom?
mom + は + how + do?
column5: どうする？ is a common question when asking someone what they're going to do (or what we should do) about some sort of dilemma.

column2: ゴスロリファッションしてみたいな。
column3: I'd like to try out goth lolita fashion.

column2: わあい！
column3: Yaay!

column2: 奢るから一緒に飲みに行かない？
column3:
Wanna go drinking together? My treat.
treat + so + together + に + drinking + に + not go?

column2: わあい！行く行く。
column3:
Yaay! I'm coming, I'm coming.
Yaay! Go + go.

column2: すごい！
column3: Amazing!

column2: あの島から泳いで来た。
column3:
I swam across from that island (over there).
that + island + from + swim + came

column2: すげー！
column3: Amazin'!

column2: よし！間に合った！
column3:
Yes! I made it!
All right! + Made it (in time)!

column2: え？今の何？
column3:
Wha? What was that just now?
Wha? + Now + の + what?
column5: This can also be used in not so pleasant situations, for example when someone says something rude.

column2: びっくりした！
column3:
That took me by surprise/scared me!
Surprise + made!

column2: 驚いた！
column3:
That took me by surprise/scared me!
Got surprised
column5: 驚いた！ Sounds a bit less casual than びっくりした！Saying びっくりした！is more common.

column2: もう死ぬかと思った！
column3:
I thought I was going to die!
soon + die + かと + thought!

column2: 信じらんない！
column3:
I can't believe this!
cannot believe!
column5: This is a casual version of the more 'grammarly' correct 信じられない（しんじられない/ cannot believe）

column2: 信じられない！
column3: I can't believe this!

column2: さっきの人ぶつかって来たのに何も言われなかった。
column3:
That person just now just bumped into me and didn't say anything.
Just now + の + person + bumped + came + even though + nothing + was said

column2: ヤダ何これ！
column3:
Oh no what is this?
Don't want to + what + this!
column5: ヤダ sounds a bit feminine. Also, a guy would be more likely to say なんだこれ！

column2: うんこ踏んじゃった！
column3:
I accidentally stepped in poop!
poop + stepped on (damn it!)

column2: 熱そうだから冷ましてから食べよう。
column3: It looks hot, so let's [so I think I'll] let it cool down a bit before eating it.

column2: 忙しそうだね。手伝おうか？
column3: You seem busy. Want me to help you?

column2: この車超高そう。
column3: This car looks really expensive.

column2: この魚、悲しそうな顔してる。
column3: This fish has a sad face.

column2: 今日嬉しそうだね。なんかあった？
column3: You seem happy today. Did something (good) happen?

column2: 気持ち悪い...吐きそう...
column3: I don't feel good... I think I'm gonna be sick...
column5: As in, "I think I'm going to vomit."

column2: 10時間も寝たのにまだ眠い。
column3:
I’m still tired [sleepy] even though I slept ten hours.
ten hours + も + slept + although + still + sleepy.

column2: せっかく水着買ったのに…
column3:
I even went to the trouble of buying a swimsuit... (This sucks!)
with trouble / for the sole purpose of / at great pains + swimsuit + bought + のに…

column2: お腹いっぱいになったら眠くなってきた。
column3:
Eating made me sleepy [tired].
stomach + full + に + if / when became + become sleepy.

column2: 寒くなった。
column3:
It got cold.
cold + became.

column2: 彼氏ができたから、人生が楽しくなった。
column3:
Life became more fun after I got a boyfriend.
boyfriend + が + was able to make + from, + life + が + fun + なった.

column2: 最初のデートは退屈だったけど、だんだんと楽しくなってきた。
column3:
Our first date was boring, but it's getting more fun now.
first + の + date + は + boring / bored + was + but, + gradually + fun + なったきた.

column2: 眠すぎて死にそう。
column3:
I’m so tired (I feel like I’m gonna die).
too sleepy + looks like I will die.

column2: 本読んでると眠くなる。
column3:
Reading makes me sleepy [tired].
book + am reading + と + sleepy + become.

column2: 食べる？
column3: Will you eat?

column2: 次の駅で乗り換えるよ。
column3: We're changing trains at the next station.

column2: 動物と遊んでると落ち着く。
column3: Playing with animals relaxes me.

column2: 冷蔵庫から豆乳出して。
column3: Take the soy milk out of the fridge.

column2: 雪が降り出した。
column3: It began to snow.
column5: Perhaps more literally, "Snow began to fall."

column2: またキャシーが変なこと言い出した。
column3: Cassie started saying weird things again.

column2: 庭の木が突然燃え出した。
column3: The tree in the garden suddenly caught on fire.

column2: 私は、列車が動き出すのを感じた。
column3:
I felt the train start to move.
I + は + train + が + start to move + のを + felt.

column2: スピーカーから音楽が流れ出した。
column3: Music started coming out of the speakers.

column2: この辺りは良質な温泉が沸き出す。
column3: There are some good hot springs around here.
column5: More literally, "In this area, high-quality onsen gush out."

column2: 炎が窓から噴き出した。
column3:
Flames shot out of the window.
flames + が + window + from + spouted.
column5: Since we're talking about something emerging naturally, we could also use the verb suffix ～出る（でる）instead of ～出す（だす）.

column2: びんが割れてワインが流れ出した。
column3:
The wine flowed out of the broken bottle.
bottle + が + broken + wine + が + flowed out
column5: Since we're talking about something emerging naturally, we could also use the verb suffix ～出る（でる）instead of ～出す（だす）.

column2: みんなでベッドを部屋から押し出した。
column3: We all pushed the bed out of the room together.

column2: 押し入れから布団を引き出した。
column3: I pulled the futon out of the closet.
column5: This the Japanese "futon"--the one you sleep on. It's not a couch.

column2: ポケットからハンカチを取り出した。

column5: A lot more people in Japan use handkerchiefs than where I came from.

column2: 未来の目標の計画を書き出す。
column3:
Write out a plan for your future goals.
future + の + goals + の + plan + を + write out.

column2: すぐに答えを考え出した。
column3:
I came up with the answer right away.
instantly + answer + thought out.

column2: "京都市左京区のピンポイント天気"
column3:
Kyoto City, Sakyo Ward’s pinpoint weather.
Kyoto + city + Sakyo + ward + の + pinpoint + weather

column2: "今日明日の天気"
column3: Today and tomorrow’s weather

column2: "３時間天気"
column3: Three hour weather

column2: "１時間天気"
column3: One hour weather

column2: "１０日間天気"
column3: Ten day weather

column2: 明日の午前は空いてますか？
column3: Do you have any openings for tomorrow morning?
column5: For example, you might say this when scheduling an appointment at the doctor or dentist.

column2: 午後から曇りだって。
column3: They're saying that it'll be cloudy from this afternoon on.

column2: ここに日付とサインをお願いします。
column3: Please sign and date here.

column2: もうすぐ離陸の時間だ。
column3: We'll be taking off soon.
column5: That is, the airplane will be taking off.

column2: 今日の気温何度？
column3: What is the temperature today?

column2: 降水確率100％だって。
column3: Apparently there is a 100% chance of rain.

column2: 梅雨の時期は降水量が多くなる。
